en: I worship the state of Tripād-Nārāyaṇa, Rāmacandra, whose form is bliss, who is the object of knowledge through the Saubhāgyalakṣmī-Kevalya-Vidyā, and who is the embodiment of auspicious fortune and prosperity.
Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech; be manifest and clear to me.
Be the two nostrils for my Veda; may what I have heard not be lost to me.
By means of this study, I join together the days and nights. I shall speak the Ṛta;
I shall speak the Truth.
May that protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
Hari Oṃ. Then the gods said to the Blessed One:
"O Blessed One, tell us the Saubhāgyalakṣmī-vidyā.
"So be it," the Blessed Ādinārāyaṇa replied, and all the gods [listened].
Listen with attentive minds to her who is the form of the Fourth (Turīya), who transcends the Fourth (Turīyātītā), who is most exalted above all,
who is seated upon the throne of all mantras, and who is surrounded by the deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha) and secondary seats (upapīṭha).

One should meditate upon Śrī, who has four arms and is golden-hued, with these fifteen verses. Now, [the lineage] of this Śrīsūkta consisting of fifteen verses is: Ānanda, Kardama, Ciklīta, and Indirāsuta.
The Seers: The seers of the fourteen verses beginning with "Śrīṛṣi" are Ānanda and others.
The meter of the first triad beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇā" is Anuṣṭubh.
The meter of "kāṃsosmi" is Bṛhatī;
that of the other two is Triṣṭubh; again, for the eight-syllable [verse] it is Anuṣṭubh;
and for the remainder it is Prastārapaṅkti. The deity is Śrī-Agni.
"Hiraṇyavarṇām" is the seed-syllable (bīja). "Kāṃso 'smi" is the power (śakti).

The ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) is performed with the mantras "Hiraṇmayā," "Candrā," "Rajatasrajā," "Hiraṇyā," and "Hiraṇyavarṇā," preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "Namaḥ," each in the dative case.

Now follows the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) by means of the three faces. One should perform the assignment in sequence upon the head, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, throat, two arms, heart, navel, private parts, anus, thighs, knees, and shanks, using the very hymns of the *Śrīsūkta*. [She is] seated upon a reddish lotus.

May Śrī, the mother of all worlds— whose complexion is like a mass of gold-dust, who holds in her lotus-hands the wish-granting gem (iṣṭa) and the pair of gestures of fearlessness (abhaya), and who is adorned with a multitude of ornaments such as jeweled bracelets—
constantly grant us prosperity. || 1 ||
In the pericarp of that pedestal is the seed-syllable of Śrī together with the object of attainment (*sādhya*).

In the eight lotuses of the Vasus and Ādityas are the half-verses and quarter-verses from the *Śrīsūkta*. Outside of that, one should [place] the mantra "yaḥ śuciḥ," the Mātṛkā, and the ten limbs of the Yantra for Śrī.
And having drawn [the image], one should invoke Śrī. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (of the deity);

the second of the lotus and other symbols; the third of her garments and ornaments; and the fourth enclosure consists of her weapons. The invocation and other rites are performed with the Śrīsūktas. There is a recitation of sixteen thousand [mantras].
The single-syllable mantra *Saubhāgyarām* has Bhṛgu as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *nicṛt* metre, and the *gāyatrī* meter; Śrī is its deity.

*Śam* is the seed-syllable and the power (*śakti*). *Śrīm* and so forth constitute the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). May she—who possesses two lotuses, whose hands grant fearlessness and boons, who shines with the luster of molten gold, and who rests upon a pair of white clouds—be ever present.

May the Goddess Śrī, who dwells upon the chest of the lotus-navelled Lord, who holds two water-pots in her hands from which she is being sprinkled with water, whose crown is bound by a stream of red [saffron], who is richly adorned with spotless silken garments and saffron unguents, who has lotus-eyes, and who rests within a lotus— may she grant us prosperity! 1.

That pedestal consists of an eight-petaled lotus, three circles, twelve segments representing the zodiac signs, and a square; this is the pedestal of Ramā. In the pericarp is the seed-syllable of Śrī together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya).
[The powers are] Vibhūti, Unnati, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kīrti, Sannati, and Vyūṣṭi.

One should worship the nine Śaktis with [the mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending in the dative case (*namaḥ*), such as *satkṛṣṭyai ṛddhyai namaḥ*. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*).
The second consists of the [mantras] beginning with Vāsudeva. The third consists of the [mantras] beginning with Bālākī.
The fourth [mantra] is addressed to Indra and the others.
There are twelve hundred thousand recitations. She is Śrī Lakṣmī, the bestower of boons, the wife of Viṣṇu, the giver of wealth, whose form is gold.
She who wears a garland of gold, she who wears a silver wreath, she whose radiance is golden, she who has golden ramparts, she who dwells in the lotus, she who holds a lotus in her hand,
she who is fond of the lotus, she who is adorned with pearls, she who is the moon and the sun, she who is fond of the *bilva* fruit, the Sovereign Goddess.
She is enjoyment, liberation, sovereign power, prosperity, abundance, attraction, nourishment, the giver of wealth,
the mistress of riches, faith, the possessor of enjoyments, the bestower of enjoyment, Sāvitrī, and the Sustainer.

The mantras beginning with "vidhātrī" and ending with "namaḥ," in the dative case, are used for the limbs and so forth, up to the seat (pīṭha), just as in the case of the single-syllable mantra. There should be one hundred thousand recitations (japa) and a tenth part thereof for libation (tarpaṇa).
The fire-oblation consists of one-tenth [of the recitation]. There is the gratification of the twice-born. Success in the Śrīvidyā belongs only to those who are free from desire;
never to those who possess desire. || 1 ||
Then the gods said to him, "Tell us the reality indicated by the fourth *māyā*. He replied, "So be it," and said:
"Yoga is to be known through yoga; yoga increases from yoga."
But that yogi who is heedful through yoga rejoices for a long time. || 1 ||
Having finished his sleep when it is worn away, eating little, and casting off fatigue and affliction in a secluded place,
he remains always free from cold and thirst; this is the effort.
Or the restraint of the vital breath [is achieved] through the path of one's own practice. || 2 ||
Having filled the mouth with air, having drawn up the *apāna* into the abode of the fire (the stomach), and having held it there by pressing the six fingers— beginning with the thumbs— of both hands,
one should likewise properly block the ears, eyes, and the pair of nostrils by this method.
Those whose minds are absorbed in various meditations on the Praṇava behold the hope of the causal conditions. || 3 ||
This must be performed by closing the ears, mouth, eyes, and nose;
then the stainless sound is clearly heard within the pure channel of the Suṣumṇā. || 4 ||
In the unstruck sound (anāhata), a resonance accompanied by various melodies is heard;
[the practitioner] possesses a divine body, is radiant, has a celestial fragrance, and is free from disease.
With a full heart, one who possesses yoga should become engaged at the beginning within the void;
having separated the second [vowel], the vital air becomes situated in the middle.
The yogi should assume a firm posture, established in the lotus or other postures;
then, from the piercing of the Viṣṇu-knot, the arising of supreme bliss occurs.
Then there arises an extremely empty *vimarda* like the sound of a kettle-drum;
having diligently pierced the third [center], there is a resonance like the sound of a *mardala* drum.
Then one proceeds to the Great Void, the foundation of all accomplishments;
then, having pierced the bliss of the mind, the wind reaches all the sacred seats.
Upon its perfection, the word "vaiṣṇava" would resound as "kvaṇa";
then the mind becomes unified, as praised by the sages Sanaka and others.
Having superimposed the infinite upon the finite and offering the partless onto the fragmentary,
one who meditates on the Plenum as primordial nature shall become fulfilled and immortal.

By means of yoga, one should immediately restrain yoga with yoga, and state with state; having thus always become the supreme reality which is free from conceptual construction, one shall become the Supreme.
Having abandoned the sense of "I" and the world-appearance which is unlike [the ultimate reality],
the wise man, established in the state free from conceptual construction, does not grieve again.
Just as rock salt attains a state of equilibrium when dissolved in water through union, so too the oneness of the self and the mind is designated as *samādhi*. (14)
When the vital breath is completely diminished and the mind dissolves, that state of equal flavor which arises is designated as samādhi. || 15 ||
That state of equality between these two— the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—
in which all volitional thoughts have entirely perished, is designated as samādhi.
That which is empty of radiance, empty of mind, empty of intellect, free from ailment,
entirely empty, and without appearance is designated as samādhi.
When the body moves by itself, the embodied soul should know that it is motionless through constant samādhi; this is called samādhi.
"Wherever the mind goes, there is the supreme state; there is the supreme Brahman, established everywhere. (19) Thus [it is said]. (2)
Then the gods said to him, "Explain the discernment of the nine wheels.

He replied, "So be it. He said: "In the foundation is the Wheel of Brahman, revolving three times, in the form of the circle of the womb. There, in the root-tuber, is the Power (Śakti) in the form of fire."
One should meditate thereon; in that very place, the seat of Kāmarūpa bestows all desires.
Thus ends the wheel of the foundation (ādhāracakra). The second is the wheel of self-perfection (svādhiṣṭhānacakra), which has six petals. In its center is a liṅga facing westward.

One should meditate on it as resembling a sprout of coral. Right there, the seat of Uḍḍiyāṇa becomes the bestower of the siddhi of attracting the world. The third is the navel-cakra, which has five whorls and the shape of a coiled serpent.

In the center of that, one should meditate upon Kuṇḍalinī, who possesses the brilliance of ten million rising suns, and whose body is slender. She is the power of capability (sāmarthya-śakti) and the bestower of all accomplishments (siddhis).
The Maṇipūra-cakra is the heart-cakra.

It has eight petals facing downwards. In its center, one should meditate on the form of a liṅga consisting of light. That indeed is the Haṃsa-kalā, beloved by all, which brings all the worlds under one's control.
The throat-cakra is four finger-breadths [in extent]. There, on the left, is the Iḍā.

The *candranāḍī* on the right is the *piṅgalā*, the solar channel; in the middle of those, one should meditate upon the *suṣumnā*, which is white in color. For one who knows this, it becomes unstruck (*anāhatā*) and bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*). There is the wheel of the palate (*tālucakra*); there flows a stream of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*).

At the throat, the root of the liṅga, and the aperture of the cakra, there is the opening suspended from the rājadanta (upper front teeth), which has ten and twelve spokes. There, one should meditate on the void; the dissolution of the mind occurs.
The seventh is the earth-cakra, the size of a thumb; therein is the eye of knowledge.
One should meditate on the form of a lamp flame; that itself bestows the accomplishment of the skull, the bulb, and speech.
The eighth is the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*). The aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) is the wheel of nirvāṇa.
There, one should meditate on a form like a smoky crest, other than the dwelling of the needle. There—
The Jālandhara-pīṭha, which bestows liberation, is the wheel of the Supreme Brahman (parabrahma-cakra).

It is the ninth, the wheel of space (ākāśa-cakra). Therein is a sixteen-petaled lotus facing upwards; its central pericarp has the form of the three peaks (trikūṭa). In its center is the upward-pointing power (ūrdhva-śakti).

Beholding her, one should meditate. Right there, the Pīṭha of Pūrṇagiri becomes the means for accomplishing all desires. He who constantly studies the Saubhāgyalakṣmī Upaniṣad becomes purified by fire; he becomes purified by wind. He...

He becomes possessed of all wealth, grain, virtuous sons, wife, horses, land, elephants, cattle, buffaloes, female slaves, and male servants, and he becomes a knower of yoga. He does not return again; he does not return again—this is the Upaniṣad.

Oṃ! May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Be manifest and auspicious to me. You two are the leaders of the Veda for me; do not abandon what I have heard. Through this study, I join together day and night. I shall speak the Truth.
I shall speak the truth. May that protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect me; may it protect the speaker; may it protect the speaker.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Śrī Saubhāgyalakṣmī Upaniṣad.
